stem.text: Define standard electrode potential, E⦵, including a description of standard conditions.

points.text:
M1 emf / potential difference / voltage
and between / compared to
and a standard hydrogen electrode and another electrode

M2 under standard conditions of
• 1 atm / 101 kPa / 100 kPa
• 298 K / 25 °C,
• (all solutions being) 1M / 1 mol dm–3 u / c

explanation.text: A standard electrode potential is always a comparison: it is the emf (voltage) measured between the half-cell of interest and a standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), the reference that is given E⦵ = 0.00 V by definition. M1 needs both electrodes mentioned (the SHE and the other electrode). M2 is unconditional (u / c) and needs all three standard conditions: 1 atm (101 or 100 kPa) for gases, 298 K, and 1 mol dm–3 for every solution.

reasoningChain: State that it is the emf / potential difference between the electrode (half-cell) and a standard hydrogen electrode.
List all three standard conditions: 1 atm, 298 K, 1 mol dm⁻³ solutions.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing 'hydrogen cell' instead of standard hydrogen electrode, which the MS guidance marks as a contradiction (CON).
Leaving out one of the three standard conditions, usually the 1 mol dm⁻³ concentration, or giving 273 K instead of 298 K.

stem.text: Table 5.1 shows the standard electrode potentials for three redox systems.
Use the information in Table 5.1 to write equations for two reactions that are feasible.
Explain why these reactions are feasible.

guidance:
A M3 two calculated Ecell
• bullet 1 Ecell = 1.53 (V)
• bullet 2 Ecell = +0.10 (V)
• bullet 3 Ecell = +1.63 (V).
I M3 use of ‘greater’ for more positive.

points.text:
M1M2
• Zn + 2Fe3+ → Zn2+ + 2Fe2+
• NO3– + 10H+ + 8Fe2+ → NH4+ + 3H2O + 8Fe3+
• NO3– + 10H+ + 4Zn → NH4+ + 3H2O + 4Zn2+
● ✓✓

M3 Ecell is positive (to be feasible)
or Eo of Fe3+ / Fe2+ and NO3– / NH4+ is more positive
or Eo of redox system 1 and 2 are more positive ora u / c

explanation.text: A reaction between two redox systems is feasible when the system with the more positive E<sup>⦵</sup> is reduced (it gains electrons, read left to right) and the system with the less positive E<sup>⦵</sup> is oxidised (read right to left). Comparing the three values: Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> (+0.77 V) can oxidise Zn (–0.76 V); NO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup>/NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (+0.87 V) can oxidise both Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Zn. That gives the three possible feasible reactions listed in the MS, and any two score M1 and M2.

Each equation must balance electrons: multiply the half-equations so that electrons lost equal electrons gained. For example, Zn loses 2e– and each Fe3+ gains 1e–, so 2Fe3+ are needed; NO3– gains 8e–, so it needs 8Fe2+ or 4Zn. The explanation (M3) is that Ecell = E(reduced) – E(oxidised) is positive, e.g. +0.77 – (–0.76) = +1.53 V, +0.87 – 0.77 = +0.10 V, +0.87 – (–0.76) = +1.63 V. The MS also accepts two calculated Ecell values for M3.

reasoningChain: Rank the three E⦵ values: +0.87 > +0.77 > –0.76 V.
Pick a pair: the more positive system is reduced, the less positive system is oxidised.
Write both half-equations in the right direction and multiply so the electrons cancel.
Add them to get the overall equation; repeat for a second pair.
Explain feasibility: E⦵cell = E⦵(reduction) – E⦵(oxidation) is positive.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing a reaction in the reverse direction, e.g. Zn²⁺ + 2Fe²⁺ → Zn + 2Fe³⁺, which has a negative E⦵cell and is not feasible.
Not balancing the electrons, e.g. Zn + Fe³⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Fe²⁺ or NO₃⁻ + 10H⁺ + Fe²⁺ → …, so the equation is unbalanced for charge.
Saying one E⦵ is 'greater' rather than 'more positive', which the MS guidance says to ignore for M3.

stem.text: Suggest why the feasible reactions in 5(b)(i) may not take place under standard conditions.

explanation.text: E⦵ values only show whether a reaction is energetically feasible; they say nothing about how fast it goes. A feasible reaction can still be too slow to observe if its activation energy is high. The MS wants the reason (high Ea), so 'the rate is too slow' on its own is ignored. 'Non-standard conditions' is also ignored, because the question already says the conditions are standard.

reasoningChain: Recall that E⦵cell predicts feasibility (thermodynamics), not rate (kinetics).
Give the kinetic reason: the activation energy of the reaction is high.

inferredMistakes.text: Answering only that 'the rate is too slow', which the MS guidance ignores because it gives no reason.
Saying the conditions are non-standard, which contradicts the question and is ignored by the MS.

markScheme.note: The MS prints an example labelled cell diagram above the nine marking bullets; shown as ms.figure, with the bullets as one point.

figure.alt: Labelled diagram of the cell: on the left H2(g) delivered to a Pt(s) electrode in H+(aq); on the right a Pt(s) electrode in NO3–(aq), H+(aq), NH4+(aq); a salt bridge joins the two beakers and a voltmeter V is connected between the two electrodes.

explanation.text: Redox system 2 has no metal in it (NO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup>, H<sup>+</sup> and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> are all ions in solution), so its half-cell needs an inert platinum electrode dipping into one solution that contains all three ions, e.g. HNO<sub>3</sub> and NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>. It is connected to a standard hydrogen electrode: H<sub>2</sub> gas bubbled through a delivery tube over a Pt electrode in H<sup>+</sup>(aq) (e.g. HCl). The two beakers are joined by a salt bridge that dips into both solutions, and the electrodes are wired to a high-resistance voltmeter.

The MS lists nine features. The annotation ● ● ✓ ● ● ✓● ● ✓ appears to mean that every group of three correct features scores 1 mark (all nine for 3 marks); this reading is an interpretation, not printed in words. A battery in the circuit contradicts the voltmeter and the complete circuit features, and graphite is accepted in place of Pt.

reasoningChain: Draw the SHE in one beaker: H⁺(aq) solution, Pt electrode, H₂ gas with a delivery tube.
Draw the other beaker: Pt electrode in a solution of NO₃⁻, NH₄⁺ and H⁺ (all labelled).
Join the solutions with a labelled salt bridge that dips into both.
Connect both electrodes through a voltmeter to complete the circuit.

inferredMistakes.text: Using a metal such as Zn or Fe as the electrode for redox system 2 instead of inert Pt, even though the system contains no metal.
Labelling the second solution with only some of the species (e.g. NO₃⁻ but not NH₄⁺ or H⁺).
Drawing a battery or power pack in the circuit, which the MS treats as a contradiction of the voltmeter and complete-circuit features.

stem.text: A different electrochemical cell is set up. The cell reaction for this electrochemical cell is shown.
Calculate the standard cell potential, E⦵cell, for this cell reaction.

explanation.text: Use ΔG⦵ = –nE⦵cellF. Here n is the number of electrons transferred in the equation as written: one Cr atom loses 3 electrons (Cr → Cr3+) and three Mn3+ ions each gain one, so n = 3. ΔG⦵ must be converted to J mol–1 (×1000) because F is in C mol–1 and V × C = J. Then E⦵cell = 645 600 ÷ (3 × 96 500) = +2.23 V. A negative ΔG⦵ goes with a positive E⦵cell, as expected for a feasible reaction.

reasoningChain: Find n = 3 from the equation (Cr → Cr³⁺ + 3e⁻).

inferredMistakes.text: Forgetting to convert kJ to J, giving 0.00223 V.
Using n = 1 (from Mn³⁺ + e⁻) instead of n = 3 for the whole equation, giving 6.69 V.
Leaving out the minus sign in ΔG⦵ = –nEF and reporting –2.23 V; the MS allows only 1 mark (ecf) for this.
